name: Unibrow trimming / bridge shaping

lead: A unibrow, or synophrys, is hair connecting the eyebrows over the bridge of the nose. Removing or shaping it makes the brows look like two separate arcs and gives a tidier, more open upper face, visible immediately.

It is a common, usually harmless polygenic trait. Cultural views differ: connected brows are admired in some historical and modern settings and not in many Western ones. No studies have tested how bridge shaping changes perceived attractiveness.

paras: People pluck, wax, thread, shave or trim the glabella hair. Plucking and waxing pull from the root and it regrows over weeks, while laser and electrolysis target the follicle for longer-lasting reduction.
Grooming can cause temporary redness, pain or ingrown hairs. Rarely, synophrys is one feature of a genetic syndrome, which is a medical rather than cosmetic matter.

chain: Brows read as two clean arcs
angle.text: Users pluck, wax, thread or shave the bridge between the brows so they read as two clean arcs and the area above the nose looks tidy. The result is visible immediately and reversible, and whether a unibrow counts as a flaw varies by culture.

lead: A unibrow, medically called synophrys, is hair that joins the two eyebrows across the glabella, the smooth area above the bridge of the nose. Unibrow trimming or bridge shaping is the grooming practice of removing or thinning that hair, by plucking, waxing, threading, shaving, or in some cases permanent hair-removal methods, so that the brows appear separate, or of deliberately keeping or shaping the bridge [1].

Synophrys is common in the general population and is usually a benign, polygenic trait, although it can also be one of several facial features in some rare genetic syndromes [1][2][3]. Cultural views of the trait vary: connected brows have been prized in some historical and contemporary settings and disfavoured in others [1][4].
infobox: Tweezing, waxing, threading, shaving, trimming; laser or electrolysis for longer-lasting removal
Polygenic trait; a GWAS in a Chinese cohort examined unibrow as one of five facial traits [2]

paras: A unibrow forms when terminal hair grows continuously across the glabella, linking the medial ends of the two brows. Density ranges from a faint line to a fully joined band [1].

Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, reports that androgens such as testosterone and dihydrotestosterone influence terminal hair density in facial regions including the glabella [1]. That page's claims are secondary and have not been independently verified here.

An Omani epidemiological study summarised by Grokipedia reported synophrys in about 11.9 percent of 927 people, more often in males, with no clear link to syndromic disorders in that group [1]. A 2022 genome-wide association study of 26,806 Chinese participants examined five aesthetic facial traits, including unibrow, and identified novel genetic associations [2].

Synophrys also appears in case reports and reviews of some rare genetic conditions, including Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, 1p36 deletion syndrome, and others, where it is one of several facial features rather than a stand-alone sign [3][5]. Transient fetal hypertrichosis and a case of bilateral milia en plaque of the eyelids with long eyelashes and unibrow have also been reported in the literature [6][7].

The Wikipedia articles on eyebrows and hair removal describe tweezing, waxing and threading as common ways to remove brow hair, and note that these can be uncomfortable for seconds or minutes [8]. Small scissors or trimmers are also used to tidy the area.

Bridge shaping in appearance communities refers to deciding how far the inner brow ends and where the gap sits, often with the aim of a clean separation between the brows. Longer-lasting options discussed elsewhere in this wiki include laser hair removal and electrolysis.

Grokipedia reports that joined brows were admired in ancient Greece and Rome, in Persian poetry, and in some contemporary Central Asian communities, while many modern Western settings treat them as less conventionally attractive, prompting removal [1]. A 2021 article in Clinics in Dermatology reviewed the societal implications of synophrys [4]. Wikipedia's eyebrow article similarly notes that a unibrow is considered attractive in some societies [8].

On looksmax.org, users post before-and-after photos of shaved unibrows and ask for ratings of the brows and eye area, with replies ranging from mixed to mildly positive. Brow grooming is generally treated as a low-cost, reversible adjustment to the eye area.

No studies found on the effect of unibrow trimming on appearance or attractiveness. Related research is limited to genetics and syndrome descriptions, such as the GWAS of aesthetic facial traits in a Chinese population [2].
